hook: Reversing a linked list never compares or swaps a single value. So what actually moves?

narration.text: A linked list is a chain of nodes, each pointing to the next. To reverse it, we walk the chain once, rewiring pointers as we go.
Three pointers do the work: prev starts at null, curr starts at the head. Each step, curr's next pointer is rewired to point back at prev.
Then prev and curr both slide one node forward, and the process repeats — one rewired pointer per node, moving steadily down the chain.
When curr finally runs off the end of the list, prev is sitting on the old last node — the new head.
Five nodes, five rewired pointers, one pass — no comparisons, no swaps, just pointers changing direction.

youtube.title: Reversing a Linked List in 30 Seconds
youtube.description: How linked list reversal really works: one pass, three pointers, and next-pointers rewired one at a time. No value comparisons or swaps involved.
